question: Can the pickup task be solved at all in our simulator? Take learning out and let a script that reads the cube's true position try 15 pickups.
measure: Strict pickups out of 15. A strict grasp means both jaw pads flat on opposite faces of the cube, held through a 1 second hold. 15 = 5 start scenarios, 3 repeats each.
outcome: Not at first: the script scored zero because the simulator made a strict grasp of the 25 mm cube physically impossible. After swapping to the MuJoCo Menagerie arm model and fixing one controller bug, it passed 15/15.
setup: A policy is the network that drives the arm. For months, policies trained with reinforcement learning (RL: try, get reward, adjust) only pinched the cube by a corner and dropped it. A privileged controller is a hand-written script that cheats: it reads the cube's exact position from the simulator, which a real policy cannot do. The project calls this test the preflight. If the cheating script fails, the task itself is broken. MuJoCo is the physics simulator. It decides when two objects touch using each part's collision shape. For a mesh, MuJoCo uses the convex hull: the shape you get by shrink-wrapping the part, which fills in any hollow. The rebuild plan made this preflight a gate (Phase 4) before any learning.

parts.title: Can the cheating script pick up the cube in the old simulator?
parts.why: If it can, the task is fine and the months of failure were a learning problem. If it cannot, no policy ever could have succeeded.
parts.did: Ran the preflight for the first time: 15 rollouts of the privileged controller under the pickup contract, then investigated the failure by measuring the collision geometry.

cells: Convex hull fills the jaw mouth
~15 mm phantom penetration at any grasp pose
Jaw-tip markers are off the jaws
fixed tip ~15-20 mm off; moving tip 27 mm short
Jaws are a scissor at cube size
parallel only at a 1.7-7.4 mm gap; ~26-34 degrees at 25 mm

parts.conclusion: The failure was not a controller bug. The hull put about 15 mm of invisible solid where the cube must sit, and at a 25 mm gap the jaws form a wedge that squeezes a rigid cube out. That is the corner pinch every earlier experiment saw. There is no baseline row: this part is a list of measurements.

parts.title: Does a properly built arm model fix it?
parts.why: The collision shapes were the problem, so the fix is a model with jaws split into convex pieces and pad shapes on the fingertips.
parts.did: Swapped the simulator to the MuJoCo Menagerie trs_so_arm100 model. One controller bug was left: the sign of a clearance shift was inverted, so the fixed jaw came down onto the cube. It was spotted in the live viewer. Then re-ran the preflight.

cells: Menagerie model, after the sign fix
Menagerie, full pick and place (v3 contract)

parts.conclusion: The task is solvable. The script passes 15/15 deterministically with zero safety violations, and also passes the longer contract that ends with the cube placed on a napkin.

trust.text: Before and after are not like for like: the controller was rewritten during the day, and the strict detector's corner margin went from 4 mm to 2 mm in the migration (memory note).
The run is deterministic: repeats give identical results.
The stored report artifacts/so_arm101_v2/simulation/preflight/fixed_pick_place_v3/evaluation.json has environment_proven true and 15 rollouts.
The log says a "~30 degree wedge". The findings note gives ~26-34 degrees.
Lift height: an earlier memory update says ~31.5 mm, the final tuning and the migration note say ~29.8 mm. The later value is used.
Simulation only. The Menagerie model is the SO-ARM100, and its joint map and camera were later found to differ from the real arm (experiments 19 to 21).

meaning: Every grasp result from the months before measured a physics bug, not learning. The rebuild could now continue: the simulator is proven and there is a working expert to copy. The next step (experiment 02) is to train a small network to imitate this script.
lesson: Before training anything, prove the task is solvable with a script that cheats. And check the collision model before trusting any grasp result.

log:
**TL;DR:** The simulator made the grasp physically impossible, so seven months
of RL had been training on a broken task.

**Problem.** I spent seven months using RL to train policies (SmolVLA, ACT) to
pick up a 25 mm cube in sim, and none of them could do it. Every policy just
pinched the cube by a corner and dropped it.

*How we know:* the grasp detector checks for a strict grasp (both jaw pads flat
on opposite faces of the cube), and across 12,000-episode runs it never fired
once. What we didn't know was whether the learning was broken or the sim was.

**Experiment.** Take learning out of the picture. I wrote a privileged
controller, basically a script that cheats by reading the cube's exact position
from the sim, and had it try 15 pickups.

*What we hope to learn:* if the cheating script can do it, the task is fine and
the problem is learning. If it can't, no policy ever could have.

**Outcome.** The cheating script failed too. Turns out the sim itself made the
grasp impossible:

- MuJoCo collides meshes using their convex hull (think shrink-wrap). The jaw is
  C-shaped, so the hull filled in the gripper's mouth with ~15 mm of invisible
  solid right where the cube goes.
- The jaws only close parallel at a 2-7 mm gap. At 25 mm they make a ~30 degree
  wedge that squeezes the cube out like a watermelon seed.

I switched to the MuJoCo Menagerie arm model, which lots of people already use
and has properly built collision shapes. One controller bug was left, and I
found it by watching the sim: the fixed jaw was coming down on top of the cube
instead of beside it. After fixing that, the script got 15/15 strict pickups.

**Takeaway:** seven months of RL results were measuring a physics bug, not
learning. Before training anything, prove the task is solvable with a script
that cheats.
